prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, wages and the regional distribution of employment

statement.case_for: I moved my preferred configuration from B012 (my opening first place) to B027, and I did so on the substance of colleagues' attribution and maturity arguments, not on how many members ranked it first. The achievement is a conceptual and empirical reorientation of how economists understand the link from technology and trade to wages and jobs. The task framework and the skills-versus-technology lineage supply the conceptual account of why labour demand shifts. The local-labour-market trade-shock designs supply credible evidence on adjustment: effects are persistent and geographically concentrated, and the frictions are real. This speaks directly to macro and distributional questions that I care about, such as capital-skill complementarity, adjustment costs and who bears the costs of technical change. The work is mature enough, with core papers from the 1990s to the mid-2010s that have been replicated, extended and challenged for a decade or more. It also has a clear policy audience. Naming Autor, Hanson and Katz lets one citation cover both the technology strand and the trade strand, with Autor as the common thread. I now think this is a cleaner and broader claim than B012. B012 is also a major advance, but its credit is more crowded with empirical and quantitative precursors outside the credited names (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum), and it sits next to the 2008 prize.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the main weakness. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is left out by the three-name limit. Katz's contribution is the long-run skills-and-technology work, so the citation joins two literatures with different identification strategies and different co-authors. The task framework also overlaps with work associated with Acemoglu (2024 prize) and with Goldin's 2023 recognition on education, technology and wages. The magnitude and long-run persistence of the China shock remain debated, and heterogeneity across countries is real. Some members may reasonably see this as two prizes rather than one. If the Committee cannot write a single coherent citation, the case weakens.

responses.point: B027 may be seen as two separate prizes, the task and skill-premium strand and the trade-shock strand. The China-shock magnitudes have also been critiqued and vary across countries.
responses.response: I take the two-prizes worry seriously, and it is why I now name Katz alongside Autor and Hanson rather than Autor and Hanson alone. The common question is how technology and trade shift labour demand and where the adjustment lands. Autor links the strands and appears on both. The magnitude critiques qualify the size of the China shock, but I think they refine the finding of persistent, concentrated adjustment rather than overturn it. I also agree with you that attribution on the task side has many hands (Levy and Murnane), and that is a real cost of the three-name limit.

responses.point: B006 should be confined to Kiyotaki and Moore, the originators of the collateral-amplification mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the accelerator strand already partly recognised in 2022, so a wider set risks redundancy.
responses.response: I accept the attribution point. My opening included Gertler, and I now think the two-person core is cleaner because the Bernanke prize in 2022 covered part of the accelerator lineage. I still do not rank B006 first. The mechanism is foundational but mostly theoretical, with thinner direct identification than the labour-demand evidence, and the 2022 prize leaves a real question about marginal novelty. I would keep it in the discussion as a strong runner-up in macro, but I do not think its tractability and influence settle the redundancy question.

responses.point: B018 (the New Keynesian framework) is the core of how central banks think. Its influence is very large and well confirmed, though credit is spread across many people.
responses.response: We agree on importance. I ranked it fifth, and the disagreement is about attribution. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford each have a distinct claim, but Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets built the estimated, medium-scale models that made it usable. Any trio omits people whose contributions are not marginal. The 2021-23 inflation episode also keeps the framework's Phillips-curve and heterogeneity components in flux. A prize should rest on a citation we can write cleanly, and for B027 I can write one more convincingly than for B018.

responses.point: B017 gives a measurable, quantitative account of why some economies stay poor. Hsieh, Klenow and Restuccia are a coherent set, and the idea has been widely absorbed.
responses.response: I agree the framework is influential, and I ranked it, but last. Measured misallocation can reflect measurement error, markups and adjustment frictions, and the share of cross-country gaps it explains is still contested. That weakens the claim that the quantitative magnitude is established. The attribution is also awkward, because Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is a parallel contribution and Rogerson is not among the credited names. I think the case needs more settling of the measurement debate before it matches the evidence behind B027 or B012.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name, and whether Katz's skills-and-technology work and the China-shock work can be joined in one citation.
How much weight the Committee should give to the 2023 and 2024 prizes when judging the incremental claim of the task framework.
Whether B012 would be a cleaner single-discovery prize once the empirical precursors outside the credited names (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) are weighed against the 2008 trade prize.
Whether the long-run persistence of China-shock effects survives continued reanalysis.
statement.conflict_note: No personal tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile. There is a research adjacency. My own work on capital-skill complementarity and inequality (with Ohanian, Ríos-Rull and Violante) is in the same broad literature as the skills-and-technology strand, and I may favour that literature. I also co-authored with colleagues Boppart and Hassler, and with Anthony Smith, but none of these are credited in B027 or B012. I flag the connection and do not adjudicate it.
